title: Nested if: a decision inside a decision

visuals.title: Login check: ID first, then PIN (correct ID is 101, correct PIN is 1234)

goal: After this you can write an if inside another if, read nested code by its braces, avoid the dangling-else trap, and know when && is the simpler choice.
warmup: At the university gate the guard asks two questions, one after the other. First: 'Do you have a student card?' Only if the answer is yes does he ask the second question: 'Is it for this semester?' If you have no card, he never asks the second question. The second decision exists only inside the first yes. That is a nested if.
definition: A nested if is an if statement placed inside the block of another if (or else). The inner condition is tested only when the outer condition lets the program reach it. Use nesting when the second decision depends on the first one.
howItWorks: Press Play and follow the flowchart. The outer condition is tested first. If it is true, the computer enters that block and meets the inner if. If the outer condition is false, the whole inner if is skipped, and the else of the outer if runs instead. Indentation helps humans to read, but the computer only listens to braces and to this rule: an else always belongs to the nearest if above it that has no else yet. This is called the dangling else. Always use { } to make the pairing you want clear.

worked.problem: Login check: the correct ID is 101 and the correct PIN is 1234. Read an ID and a PIN. If the ID is wrong print Unknown user. If the ID is right, check the PIN: print Welcome if it is right and Wrong PIN if not.
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Read id, pin/]
  B --> C{id == 101?}
  C -->|No| D[/Print Unknown user/]
  C -->|Yes| E{pin == 1234?}
  E -->|Yes| F[/Print Welcome/]
  E -->|No| G[/Print Wrong PIN/]
  D --> H([End])
  F --> H
  G --> H

sample.title: Login: ID then PIN

explanation.text: Two whole numbers: the ID and the PIN.
Reads both values typed by the user.
Outer if: is the ID correct? The PIN is not looked at yet.
Inner if: reached only when the ID was correct.
Both ID and PIN are right.
ID is right but PIN is wrong. This else belongs to the inner if.
This else belongs to the outer if: the ID was wrong.

steps.note: cin reads 101 into id and 9999 into pin.
Outer test: is id == 101? Yes. Enter the block.
Inner test: is pin == 1234? 9999 is not 1234, so false.
The inner else runs and prints Wrong PIN. The outer else is skipped.

worked.problem: Read three different or equal numbers and print the largest of them using nested if statements.
pseudocode: IF a >= c THEN largest = a ELSE largest = c
IF b >= c THEN largest = b ELSE largest = c
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Read a, b, c/]
  B --> C{a >= b?}
  C -->|Yes| D{a >= c?}
  C -->|No| E{b >= c?}
  D -->|Yes| F[/Print a/]
  D -->|No| G[/Print c/]
  E -->|Yes| H[/Print b/]
  E -->|No| G
  F --> I([End])

  H --> I

sample.title: Largest of three numbers

explanation.text: Reads the three numbers separated by spaces.
First compare a and b. The loser of this match cannot be the largest.
a beat b, so a only has to beat c.
a lost to c, so c is the largest.
b beat or equalled a, so b only has to beat c.
c is larger than b, which was already larger than a.

steps.note: cin reads three numbers into a, b and c.
Is a >= b? Is 4 >= 19? No. Go to the else part.
Inner test in the else: is b >= c? Is 19 >= 11? Yes.
b is the largest. Print it.

worked.problem: A student passes the course only if marks are 50 or more AND attendance is 75 or more. If marks are below 50 print Fail. If marks are fine but attendance is low, print Detained: short attendance. Read marks and attendance and print the result.
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Read marks, attendance/]
  B --> C{marks >= 50?}
  C -->|No| D[/Print Fail/]
  C -->|Yes| E{attendance >= 75?}
  E -->|Yes| F[/Print Pass/]
  E -->|No| G[/Print Detained/]
  D --> H([End])
  F --> H
  G --> H

sample.title: Marks and attendance

explanation.text: Outer test on marks. Low marks mean Fail whatever the attendance is.
Reached only when marks are fine. Now check attendance.
Marks are fine but attendance is low.
Marks below 50, so the student fails.

variations.when: The second question makes sense only after the first answer is yes, or you need different messages for each failure
variations.example: if (id == 101) { if (pin == 1234) cout << "OK"; else cout << "Wrong PIN"; }

variations.when: Both must be true and one single message is enough
Extra decision only on the false side
variations.example: else { if (b >= c) cout << b; else cout << c; }

variations.when: Choices are on the same level, not dependent
Always, to stop the dangling else problem

mistakes.error: No compiler error. The else pairs with the nearest if (b > 0), not with a > 0, even though the indentation suggests otherwise.
expected '}' at end of input (one opening brace was never closed)

mistakes.wrong: if (a > b) cout << "A"; cout << "X"; else cout << "B";
mistakes.right: if (a > b) { cout << "A"; cout << "X"; } else cout << "B";

examTips: An else belongs to the NEAREST unmatched if above it, whatever the indentation shows.
Use braces { } on every nested block. It removes the dangling else problem completely.
If both conditions must be true and you print one message, a single if with && is shorter than a nested if.
Choose nesting when each failure needs its own message (Unknown user vs Wrong PIN).
To trace nested code, test the outer condition first and ignore the inner block if the outer one is false.
romanSummary: Nested if ka matlab hai if ke andar dosra if.
Andar wali condition tabhi check hoti hai jab bahar wali true ho.
else hamesha sab se qareebi if ke saath judta hai, indentation se farq nahi parta.
Braces { } hamesha lagao taake dangling else ka masla na aaye.
Agar dono conditions ek saath chahiye aur ek hi message hai to && use karna aasan hai.

practice.prompt: When is the inner condition of a nested if tested?
options: Only when the outer condition is true
Only when the outer condition is false
practice.answer: Only when the outer condition is true
practice.hint: The guard asks the second question only after the first yes.
practice.explanation: The inner if lives inside the outer if block, so it is reached only if the outer condition is true.

practice.hint: y < 15 is false, then the line after the inner if still runs because it is inside the outer block.
practice.explanation: x > 5 is true, so we enter. y < 15 is false, so the inner else prints Q. Then R prints, because it is a separate statement inside the outer block.

practice.hint: Ignore the indentation. Which if does the else belong to?
practice.explanation: The else pairs with the nearest if, which is if (b > 0). a > 0 is true, b > 0 is false, so the else runs and prints Y. If a were -1, nothing would print at all.

practice.hint: Close the inner if with braces so the else cannot join it.
practice.explanation: With braces around the inner if, the else pairs with the outer if (a > 0) as intended.

practice.prompt:
Fill in the blank to make this single if mean the same as a nested if with ID and PIN:

if (id == 101 ____ pin == 1234) cout << "Welcome";
practice.explanation: && is true only when both sides are true, just like entering the outer if and then passing the inner if.

practice.prompt: Read an integer n. If n is positive, print Positive even or Positive odd. If it is not positive, print Not positive. Use a nested if.
practice.hint: First test n > 0, then test n % 2 == 0 inside.
practice.explanation: The even/odd check makes sense only for positive numbers, so it lives inside the outer if.

options: Two if statements one after another
quiz.explanation: A nested if is placed in the block of another if or else.

quiz.prompt: An else always belongs to which if?
options: The nearest unmatched if above it
The first if in the program
The if with the biggest condition
quiz.answer: The nearest unmatched if above it
quiz.hint: This is the dangling else rule.
quiz.explanation: C++ pairs each else with the closest earlier if that does not have an else yet.

quiz.prompt: How can you avoid the dangling else problem?
quiz.explanation: Braces state clearly which if the else belongs to. Indentation does not change the meaning.

quiz.prompt: Which single line is equal to: if (a > 0) { if (b > 0) { cout << "OK"; } }
quiz.explanation: A nested if without else is the same as combining the two conditions with &&.
